To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the memory interference in an interleaved memory multiprocessor system can be characterized by the ratio of the number of memory references per instruction executed by each processor to the total number of memory modules in the system, and that the interference is a decreasing function of this ratio.

(1) The limiting behavior of the relative interference caused by multiple processors simultaneously using multiple memory modules is approximately a constant, independent of the size of the system; (2) the limiting constant is approximately equal to one-half the number of memory modules divided by the number of processors; and (3) the constant is approximately equal for a large class of systems, including those more closely approximating real systems.

, in the simple model of a multiprocessor system with interleaved memory, the degree of memory interference is approximately equal to the number of memory modules used divided by the number of processors, and that this result is valid for real systems of this class.

memory interference can be a serious problem in multiprocessor systems with interleaved memories.

the limiting behavior of memory interference in a large system is not a simple function of the number of processors or the number of memory modules, but depends on the number of memory references per instruction, the number of memory instructions per program execution, the memory reference pattern, and the memory access time.
